speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
This completes the
estimates of the Department of Forestry.

Supply-Forestry

I had contemplated making some remarks in reply to constructive suggestions put forward by members in all parts of the house. I wish to say thanks to all the speakers. I appreciate their suggestions greatly, as well as their good wishes and congratulations.
I should have said earlier that the federal-provincial forestry conference which took place on October 21 and 22, to which reference was made by two or three speakers tonight, was in my humble opinion, and in the opinion of the 10 provincial ministers who attended, a highly successful affair.
It was the first one of its kind, and to answer a question put by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, they suggested that meetings be held at least once a year. ARDA, among other matters, was discussed at some length, and has general support, particularly in the provinces of New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario.
There was also general agreement that on the whole the federal-provincial forestry agreements which have been in effect for the past 12 years have been successful. The ministers did plead for greater flexibility because of the different topographic and geographic conditions that exist in the east, and which differ from those in the west. More planes may be needed in a province like British Columbia, and more access roads in Ontario and Quebec, where the terrain is entirely different. There was unanimity on the general merits of these agreements.
There was also unanimity on the submission that there should be greater research, and there was assurance of full co-operation among all 10 provinces. One could not have asked for a better atmosphere or for more co-operation. Of course there were a few disagreements, and that is why the meeting was held in camera. It was closed to the press. Some hon. members have commented that they did not see any publicity about it. A press release was issued on the second night of the conference, and there was a press conference; but as hon. members will recall, we had some competition that day. It was the day the S.I.U. visited parliament hill, and they, rather than the 11 ministers of forestry drew most of the members of the press.
Was there any discussion at this conference about the relative merits of putting federal money into the provincial agreements, as opposed to expanding the research services?

No, they wanted more money for both, but I was not in a position to commit myself. I told them their views would be taken into consideration and placed before my colleagues in the government.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
One other matter to which perhaps I should have referred earlier was raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West, among others. He stressed the necessity of interesting the youth of Canada-of educating them in the importance of the forest industry. This is of the utmost importance. I cannot commend too highly the junior forest warden movements in certain provinces, particularly Ontario and British Columbia where they have had great success. There has also been work of a similar nature by 4-H clubs in Quebec, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and I commend this work very highly.
Two years ago the provinces signed an agreement to build roads to forests, and I would like to know if the provinces, particularly Quebec, expressed their views about renewing this agreement?

I can only refer to the press conference and the statement that was made on the subject. It was stated by the 10 ministers, including the minister from Quebec, that the federal-provincial agreements had on the whole been successful. The Quebec minister agreed that these agreements, which cover not only access roads but forest inventory and reforestation, had been more or less satisfactory. He said that the province of Quebec was willing to consider renewal of the agreement on the same general basis as the other provinces, but he said there had been certain reservations made by the premier of Quebec with regard to federal-provincial agreements generally, and these would have to be the subject of further discussion with the federal government.
I asked the question because Mr. Arsenault, the former minister of forestry, was opposed to these joint progams.

Mr. Chairman, as I rise to speak on the estimates of the Department of Public Works, I wish first of all to congratulate the minister (Mr. Deschatelets) for the honour his leader has conferred upon him, by asking him to take the lead of one of the key departments.
However, I am saddened by the thought that the Prime Minister had some misgivings about the qualifications of the nominee, and about the time he might be ready and willing

to spend on matters coming under his jurisdiction. It is also a pity that the Prime Minister has seen fit to remove from the scope of that jurisdiction the administration of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I would have liked us to remain faithful to tradition on that point. Things being what they are, I can only extend my heartfelt sympathy to the minister, who probably also feels some regret at seeing his powers and responsibilities thus whittled away.
Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for the courtesy with which he has always listened to my suggestions about changes to be brought to inscriptions and signs on parliament hill, inside parliament itself and within various federal buildings. When I suggested replacing signs in one language only by signs written both in English and in French, the minister followed in the footsteps of his predecessors, who never failed to comply with my requests.
Actually, Mr. Chairman, it is not without a certain pride that I remind the house that when I came to Ottawa in 1957, as a member for the St. Hyacinthe-Bagot riding, most notices on doors and elsewhere on parliament hill, were written in one language only, that is to say in English.
At that time, I tried hard to make some recommendations which resulted in those bilingual notices that can now be seen almost everywhere, instead of unilingual ones.
Mr. Chairman, I wanted to mention the fact incidentally, because I think it is better to keep in the background while working and then succeed, than to make a lot of noise, as has been heard for the past couple of years, with only indifferent results.
Mr. Chairman, I also want to take this opportunity to pay tribute to the officials who assist the minister in his work. They are most understanding and have always given me a maximum of co-operation when I approached them with requests. Indeed, I know from my own experience that when reasonable requests are made to the Minister of Public Works or his officials, they are always quite ready to help and have only one object, that is to give the best possible service to the people.
And how could it be otherwise, when we consider that, since I have come to the house I succeeded in convincing the officials of that department that certain projects should be carried out in my riding, at a cost of $1,200,000? Mr. Chairman, I point out those facts without boasting and without excessive humility, whether it pleases my good friend from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) or not.
I think that without the co-operation of the present minister's predecessors and of the
Supply-Public Works
officials, I certainly would not have achieved such results.
In his introductory remarks on his estimates, the minister made a brief review of the situation he found in his department when he took over. He indicated that the estimates were prepared by his predecessor and he did not see the need for a detailed analysis of them. But we would have liked him to take a little more time and give us the reasons for the statement he made on October 18 last, as can be seen on page 3760 of Hansard where the minister stated:
However, we have slightly changed those estimates and to enable the house to get a better understanding of the various projects and amounts you are called upon to approve, I intend to give you some essential explanations and I will do it alternatively in French and in English.
Mr. Chairman, may I point out that I have read this statement of the minister several times, and it may be that I cannot read between the lines, but I find no justification the minister might have given for the cancelling some items or affecting additional amounts to other projects. In fact, the minister told us he had cancelled some $2.5 million, while he asked us to pass additional projects for some $6.3 million.
We would have liked the minister to tell us-and we were entitled to know-which projects he thought it was his duty to cancel and what additional projects he added, as well as the reasons justifying those cancellations or additions to the budgetary estimates for the current year.
I find it a little difficult to understand why the officials, after thinking out the plans of the previous administration, were not somewhat aggrieved at the decision of the minister to make such large cuts in the estimates they had prepared for the year 1962-63. Those officials are known for their broadmindedness and their impartiality as well as for their desire to serve the people, and surely until the time the present minister took over the department, those officials did their best in the preparation of their work.
Unless the minister gives us the reasons why he decided to make the changes, we are entitled to wonder on certain obscure points.
Mr. Chairman, as it is the first time that I address myself to the Minister of Public Works since he assumed his post, I shall avail myself of the opportunity to utter a few requests in order to improve the postal services in my constituency. Those requests will also tend to reduce unemployment which prevails in my constituency, for, as you know, Mr. Chairman, my constituency is not different from the others.

Supply-Public Works
Among all the provinces in this country, the province of Quebec unfortunately holds the sad record of having the greatest number of unemployed.
I trust that the minister, who, also, comes from the province of Quebec and wishes sincerely the good of its inhabitants, will not hesitate to give me his help and his cooperation in order that, together we may secure employment for the heads of families who surely need work to meet their responsibilities.
In order to reduce unemployment in my constituency, I suggest to the Minister of Public Works to build post offices in the villages of St. Denis sur Richelieu and St. Rosalie, in Bagot county, St. Damase, in St. Hyacinthe county, and in Upton, in Bagot county. Those four places are big enough and important enough, it seems to me, to have their own post offices. In so doing, the minister would certainly enhance the pride of the citizens of those municipalities. In any village or rural community, people are always proud to say: we are important enough to have our federal building. That is why I am asking for the minister's support in this field.
I have another suggestion to make to the minister. It has to do with giving a slightly more bilingual appearance to the uniforms worn by messengers and persons who run elevators one comes across in the parliament buildings. As a matter of fact, I sent a letter to the minister to this effect.
At the present time, if you look at those uniforms, you only see three letters, "D.P.W.", which stand for "Department of Public Works".
I should like to see the practice which is applied to the uniforms worn by the parliament buildings' constables also adopted in the case of those employees of the Department of Public Works, that is to say, place on one side or on one shoulder, for instance, the letters D.P.W. and, on the other one, the letters M.T.P. to identify employees of the Department of Public Works. That is a suggestion I offer to the minister, and since we know he also wants to do his share in the field of bilingualism, he will surely not miss an opportunity to follow that suggestion.
And now, Mr. Chairman, I must, much to my regret but it is imperative, come to another matter which will probably not please so much the Minister of Public Works. It is about patronage that I want to talk to the minister for a few moments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: That is a fine matter.

According to the information in my possession, it has been decided lately to increase from $5,000 to $15,000 the amount

of contracts awarded on invitation only. I would be happy to learn from the minister whether this information is true and if it is, could he tell me who supplies the list of tenderers for such work.
Moreover,' I wonder if the minister could tell us who is responsible for supplying the names of persons who could become inspectors on the building site of sustaining walls. And before going further, may I remind the minister that I sent him two letters recommending some persons who could act as inspectors on these building sites.
The people I recommended are qualified and they have a vast experience in that field, having already held the position of inspectors for several years, in addition to their experience they have earned a reputation for impartiality. Unfortunately, and to my great surprise, I have learned that people other than those I recommended were chosen to supervise the construction of the retaining walls in St. Denis sur Richelieu and St. Charles sur Richelieu.

May I ask the hon. member
a question?

Certainly, but when I have completed my remarks which will only take me a few minutes more.
I should like very much to know why the people I recommended were not hired and from whom did the Minister of Public Works get the names of the people concerned.
Maybe he could also tell me what is the part played by my opponent in the last general election, Mr. Jean Leduc of Ste. Pie. According to the information I have, the property purchased by the Department of Public Works as a possible site for the penitentiary that was to be built in Ste. Pie, was the scene of a dramatic sale of hay last summer. I am informed that Mr. Leduc was the person authorized to conduct the sale of hay. Since this individual was defeated in the last general election, it is very strange that he should carry out a duty which, in my opinion, should belong to the representative elected by the people. I should like to know very much who gave him this authority and who recommended him as such.
Could it be that there is a list of consultants as there is in the Post Office Department where I saw the name of Mr. Leduc?
Actually, I would not be surprised if his name should appear on another list, and it is for this reason that I would like the Minister of Public Works to confirm or deny my statements.
It is likely the same list.

Mr. Chairman, the minister is aware that a penitentiary was to be erected

in my riding, more specifically in the parish of St. Pie de Bagot. I can only mention the matter this evening, since I will have an opportunity later on to discuss it when we examine the various estimates of the department.
As I have not as yet succeeded in securing a satisfactory reply from the Department of Justice, I would appreciate it if the Minister of Public Works, who is undoubtedly aware of the situation, since it is his department which acquired the land, would supply me with certain information.
For instance, what use will be made of that land which was purchased at the price of $83,000? What are the reasons which motivated the transfer of the proposed penitentiary to another riding?
I feel that the question concerns the minister since the construction of penitentiaries comes under his department.
In view of the fact that I have been unable to get a satisfactory reply from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier), I hope the Minister of Public Works will be more co-operative than his colleague and provide me with all the information I am entitled to since it would be interesting to know why, after last April 8, it was suddenly decided to give up the proposed construction of a penitentiary at St. Pie de Bagot.
Mr. Chairman, I have here some documents which prove without question and according to the plans of the Departments of Justice and Public Works, since there is a double jurisdiction in the matter, that the work should normally be under way. Why has it not started? I was unable to find out up to now, and I ask the minister to tell me.
With further reference to the selection of inspectors and to their duties, I would like the minister to tell me also whether the inspector who represents the federal government on the building site of a retaining wall must remain on the spot or whether he may stay away and, in that case, for how long during the day. I am asking the minister whether an inspector may leave his job and meet at the same time the requirements of the Department of Public Works.
If I seek that information, it is in the interest of the Department of Public Works and of the general public. In fact, I would say that in order to do his work properly, a supervisor should be on the site all day long and not only part of the time.
The answers to those few questions will put me straight and enable me, at the same time, to relay information to those who ask me for it, because I make it a point to keep the minister aware of the way the work is proceeding with regard to the erection of the 28902-5-277
Business of the House
retaining walls. Those are all questions that people are asking themselves.
I would not want to offend the minister but I must tell him that patronage is being practiced on a large scale and that probably he would not put up with it if he really wanted to stop it. However, I feel duty bound to tell him. A lot of patronage is going on now with regard to the work at St. Charles and at St. Denis sur Richelieu. I would not want to stir up memories, but-
I understand why-

May I ask a question of my hon. friend?
He just mentioned the work under way concerning the sustaining walls. The hon. member asserted that some sort of patronage was taking place. I would like to have more details in order to be able to reply adequately. I do not suppose my hon. friend would make such assertions without knowing certain facts. I ask him then to give me a few facts.

Mr. Chairman, I would have preferred not to mention that. I merely wanted to warn the minister in private. But since he raises the question, I have no alternative but to justify my allegations.
I will refer to letters which I wrote to him under date of June 24, concerning the appointment of inspectors. I recommended three persons for St. Denis and St. Charles, but none of them was hired. Those who were hired as inspectors had been recommended by Liberal organizers in both the above-mentioned villages. This is one example, Mr. Chairman. If you want more I could state others because, in my opinion, one can achieve the same purpose without bringing up the past.

Mr. Chairman, before
starting my remarks I should like to congratulate the Minister of Public Works on his appointment to this department.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it 10.30?
